english: I'm going to the market with a friend today.
grammar: 랑 (rang) = 'with/and' after a vowel: 친구랑 (chingu-rang = with a friend).

english: I buy fruit and vegetables at the market.
grammar: 과 (gwa) = 'and' after a consonant: 과일과 야채 (gwail-gwa yachae = fruit and vegetables).

english: The mart is close to my house.
The convenience store is open 24 hours.
I look around at the department store.
grammar: 구경해요 (gugyeonghaeyo) = look around, browse — shopping without buying.
팔다 (palda) = to sell: 옷을 팔아요 (os-eul parayo = sells clothes). To buy = 사다 (sada).

english: I buy milk at the convenience store.
The market is cheaper than the mart.
grammar: N보다 (boda) = 'than N': 마트보다 싸요 (mateu-boda ssayo = cheaper than the mart).

english: On weekends the department store is crowded.
grammar: 많다 (manta) = to be many: 사람이 많아요 (saram-i manayo = it's crowded).

english: This market is famous for its fish.
The store opens at ten in the morning.
The mart closes at ten at night.
I buy ramyeon and gimbap at the convenience store.
There's a new store over there.
grammar: 새 (sae) = 'new' before a noun: 새 가게 (sae gage = a new store).
Prices use Sino numbers + 원 (won): 만 원 (man won = 10,000 won).
오만 (oman) = 50,000: 오 (o = five) times 만 (man = ten thousand).
오백 (obaek) = 500: 오 (o = five) + 백 (baek = hundred).
개 (gae) counts things with NATIVE numbers: 다섯 개 (daseot gae = five items).
만 오천 (man ocheon) = 15,000 — stack 만 (10,000) + 오천 (5,000).

english: Please give me a little discount.
grammar: 깎아 주세요 (kkakka juseyo) = 'please lower the price' — fine at markets, not at malls.

english: At the market, people haggle over prices.
The price is a bit expensive.
grammar: 좀 (jom) softens statements: 좀 비싸요 (jom bissayo = it's a bit expensive).
세일 (seil) = sale, from English; 세일해요 (seilhaeyo) = it's on sale.

english: The department store is having a sale now.

grammar: N 중이에요 (jung-ieyo) = 'in the middle of N': 세일 중이에요 (seil jung-ieyo = it's on sale).
만 (man) after a noun = 'only': 오늘만 (oneul-man = today only) — same sound as 만 = 10,000!
였어요 (yeosseoyo) = 'was' after a vowel: 얼마였어요? (eolma-yeosseoyo = how much was it?)
Past adds ㅆ: 비싸요 → 비쌌어요 (bissasseoyo = was expensive).
더 (deo) = more: 더 쌌어요 (deo ssasseoyo = was cheaper).
쓰다 (sseuda) = write, use, AND spend: 돈을 썼어요 (don-eul sseosseoyo = spent money).
색 (saek) = color: 무슨 색 (museun saek = what color).
Color words end in -색 (saek): 파란색 (paransaek = blue).
예쁘다 → 예뻐요 (yeppeoyo = is pretty): the ㅡ drops before 어요.

english: Do you have a yellow umbrella?
Do you have a different color?
grammar: 다른 (dareun) = another/different before a noun: 다른 색 (dareun saek = a different color).

english: I'm buying a skirt and pants.
That T-shirt has a pretty color.

grammar: 쓰다 also = wear on your head: 모자를 써요 (moja-reul sseoyo = I wear a hat).
새로 (saero) = newly, anew: 새로 샀어요 (saero sasseoyo = newly bought).

english: I buy socks at the market.

grammar: ㅂ-verbs soften: 가볍다 → 가벼워요 (gabyeowoyo = is light).
어울리다 = to suit: 저한테 어울려요 (jeohante eoullyeoyo = it suits me).

english: I'm buying a scarf as a present.
grammar: 선물 (seonmul) = present, gift: 선물로 (seonmul-lo = as a gift).

english: This clothing store has cheap T-shirts.

grammar: V-어 봐요 = 'try V-ing': 입어 봐요 (ibeo bwayo = try it on). 봐요 works as its own helper word.
신다 (sinda) = wear on your FEET: 신발을 신어요 (sinbal-eul sineoyo = wear shoes).

english: I tried on pants at the store.
grammar: 봐요 → 봤어요 (bwasseoyo): 입어 봤어요 (ibeo bwasseoyo = tried it on).

english: This size is too small for me.
grammar: 한테 (hante) = 'to/for (a person)': 저한테 작아요 (jeohante jagayo = small for me).

english: These pants are a bit big.
The shoes are a little small.
grammar: 조금 (jogeum) = a little; 좀 (jom) is its casual short form.
맞다 (matda) = to fit, be right: 사이즈가 맞아요 (saijeu-ga majayo = the size fits).

english: The dress suited you really well.
The fitting room is over there.

grammar: 한번 (hanbeon) softens suggestions: 한번 입어 봐요 (hanbeon ibeo bwayo = just try it on).

english: I tried on these dress shoes.

grammar: 길다 (gilda) = to be long: 치마가 길어요 (chima-ga gireoyo = the skirt is long).

english: The pants are a little short.
grammar: 짧다 (jjalda) = to be short: 바지가 짧아요 (baji-ga jjalbayo = the pants are short).

english: We don't have that size right now.
These shoes are comfortable on the feet.
grammar: 편하다 (pyeonhada) = comfortable: 발이 편해요 (bar-i pyeonhaeyo = easy on the feet).
손님 (sonnim) = guest, customer — how shop staff politely address you.

english: Sorry, those clothes are not on sale.

grammar: N(으)로 = 'by, with': 카드로 계산해요 (kadeu-ro gyesanhaeyo = pay by card).
현금 (hyeongeum) = cash; 카드 (kadeu) = card — the checkout question pair.

english: Please give me the receipt too.

grammar: 돼요 (dwaeyo) = 'it's possible': 환불이 돼요? (hwanbur-i dwaeyo? = is a refund possible?)

english: I got a refund for these clothes.
grammar: 환불 (hwanbul) = refund; 환불해요 (hwanbulhaeyo) = get or give a refund.
바꾸다 → 바꿔요 (bakkwoyo = exchange, change): 우 + 어 contracts to 워.

english: Can I exchange these pants for a different size?

grammar: 봉투 (bongtu) = shopping bag, envelope — cashiers ask 봉투가 필요해요?
하나 (hana) = one, standing alone; before a counter it becomes 한 (han).
점원 (jeomwon) = store clerk; 친절해요 (chinjeolhaeyo) = is kind.
물어봐요 (mureobwayo) = ask (and see) — 봐요 again as a helper.
또 (tto) = again: 또 올 거예요 (tto ol geoyeyo = I'll come again).

english: Yesterday I bought fruit at the market.
grammar: Past = ㅆ + 어요: 사요 → 샀어요 (sasseoyo = bought).

english: Last weekend I went to the department store.
grammar: 지난 (jinan) = last, past: 지난 주말 (jinan jumal = last weekend).
벌 (beol) counts clothes: 치마 두 벌 (chima du beol = two skirts).

english: I bought a pair of shoes.
grammar: 켤레 (kyeolle) counts pairs of shoes: 한 켤레 (han kyeolle = one pair).

english: Yesterday I spent a lot of money.
grammar: 많이 (mani) = a lot: 많이 썼어요 (mani sseosseoyo = spent a lot).

english: I bought that watch on sale.
Last week I bought this coat.
grammar: 지난주 (jinanju) = last week — one word, no space.

english: I haggled the price down at the market.

grammar: 받다 (batda) = to receive: 선물을 받았어요 (seonmur-eul badasseoyo = received a gift).

english: Tomorrow I'll go to the mart.
grammar: Future = stem + ㄹ 거예요: 가다 → 갈 거예요 (gal geoyeyo = will go).

english: This weekend I'll buy new clothes.
grammar: 살 거예요 (sal geoyeyo) = will buy — from 사다 (sada), not 살다 (salda = live)!

english: Next week I'll go to the market.
grammar: 다음 (daeum) = next: 다음 주 (daeum ju = next week).

english: I'll buy a birthday present for my friend.
I'll look around at the department store.

grammar: 볼 거예요 (bol geoyeyo) = will see, will try: 입어 볼 거예요 (ibeo bol geoyeyo = will try it on).

english: I'll spend only a little money.
I'll buy sneakers in the sale.
Next month I'll exchange the bag.
grammar: 달 (dal) = month (and moon): 다음 달 (daeum dal = next month).
우리 (uri = our) is how Koreans say 'my' for family: 우리 가족 (uri gajok = my family).

english: Do you have a family photo?

grammar: 부모님 (bumonim) = parents; the -님 (nim) adds respect.

english: My father works at a company.

grammar: 잘 + verb = do well: 요리를 잘해요 (yori-reul jalhaeyo = cooks well).
언니 (eonni) = older sister for a FEMALE speaker. Men say 누나 (nuna).

english: My older sister is three years older than me.

grammar: 누나 (nuna) = older sister for a MALE speaker — 민수 (a man) says 누나.

target: 준호 씨는 형이 두 명 있어요.
grammar: 형 (hyeong) = older brother for a MALE speaker. Women say 오빠 (oppa).
오빠 (oppa) = older brother for a FEMALE speaker — 수진 (a woman) says 오빠.
동생 = younger sibling: 남동생 (namdongsaeng = brother), 여동생 (yeodongsaeng = sister).

english: My younger sister is a university student.
My younger sibling is at school now.

grammar: 계세요 (gyeseyo) = honorific 'is (there)' for elders; the plain form is 있어요 (isseoyo).

english: My grandfather is at home now.

grammar: 드세요 (deuseyo) = honorific 'please eat' for elders; the plain form is 먹어요 (meogeoyo).
이모 (imo) = aunt on Mom's side — Korean kinship words mark the exact relation.
사촌 (sachon) = cousin — literally 'four degrees' of kinship distance.

english: We also have a puppy at home.
My husband works at a bank.

grammar: 아내 (anae) = my wife; another person's wife is politely 부인 (buin).
결혼했어요 (gyeolhonhaesseoyo) — Korean uses past 'got married' for 'is married'.

english: My older brother is still a student.
My older brother got married last week.

grammar: 과/와 (gwa/wa) = 'with, and': 부모님과 (bumonim-gwa = with my parents).

english: My older sister works at a hospital.
My whole family is in Seoul.
I talk on the phone with my younger sister every day.
My family cooks together on weekends.
I meet my family on Sunday.

grammar: 키가 커요 (ki-ga keoyo) = 'is tall' — literally 'height is big'.
머리 (meori) = head AND hair: 머리가 짧아요 (meori-ga jjalbayo = has short hair).

english: My younger sibling has big eyes.
The baby's hands are really small.

grammar: 쓰다 also covers glasses: 안경을 써요 (angyeong-eul sseoyo = wears glasses).

english: That actor has a small face.
grammar: Koreans compliment 얼굴이 작아요 (eolgur-i jagayo = 'your face is small') — it means good-looking!
마음이 따뜻해요 (maeum-i ttatteuthaeyo) = warm-hearted — 마음 = heart, mind.

english: My younger sibling has a nice personality.

grammar: 닮았어요 (dalmasseoyo) = resemble — always in the past form: 아빠를 닮았어요 (I take after Dad).

english: My younger sister looks like Mom.
My older brother and I look really alike.

grammar: 그분 (geubun) = respectful 'that person' — politer than 그 사람 (geu saram).
아직 (ajik) = still, yet: 아직 젊어요 (ajik jeolmeoyo = still young).
세다 (seda) = to be strong: 힘이 세요 (him-i seyo = is strong).

english: My older sister's hair is brown.

grammar: 착해요 (chakaeyo) = kind-hearted, well-behaved — the go-to praise for kids.

english: My son is good at sports.
My cousin is the same age as me.
grammar: 같아요 (gatayo) = is the same: 나이가 같아요 (nai-ga gatayo = same age).

english: I don't know that person's name.

grammar: 살 (sal) counts age with native numbers: 몇 살이에요? (myeot sar-ieyo? = how old are you?)
스무 (seumu) = twenty before a counter: 스무 살 (seumu sal = 20 years old).

english: My younger sibling is eight years old.
grammar: 여덟 (yeodeol) = eight (native number): 여덟 살 (yeodeol sal = eight years old).

english: Our baby is two years old.
How old are you, if I may ask?
grammar: 나이가 어떻게 돼요? (nai-ga eotteoke dwaeyo?) = polite 'how old are you?' — softer than 몇 살이에요?
생일 축하해요 (saengil chukahaeyo) = happy birthday — literally 'I congratulate your birthday'.

english: There's a birthday party on Saturday.
I'm inviting friends to the party.
grammar: -들 (deul) makes plurals: 친구들 (chingu-deul = friends). Korean often skips it.

english: I invited my older sister to the party.
I got a book as a birthday present.
My friends are singing a song.
grammar: 부르다 → 불러요 (bulleoyo = sing, call): 르-verbs double the ㄹ.

english: I got a watch on my birthday last year.
I'll have a party on my birthday next year.

grammar: 처음 뵙겠습니다 (cheoeum boepgetseumnida) = formal 'nice to meet you' — 합니다체, for first meetings.

english: It's really nice to meet you.

grammar: 이분 (ibun) = polite 'this person' — use it to introduce someone respectfully.
이쪽은 (ijjog-eun) = 'this side is...' — a natural way to introduce someone.
왔어요 (wasseoyo) = came: 어디에서 왔어요? (eodieseo wasseoyo? = where are you from?)

english: When did you come to Korea?

grammar: 잘 지내요? (jal jinaeyo?) = 'how are you?' — literally 'are you getting along well?'

english: Did you have a good weekend?
It's been such a long time!
grammar: 오랜만이에요 (oraenman-ieyo) = 'long time no see' — literally 'it's been a while'.

english: Is it your first time here?
grammar: 처음 (cheoeum) = first time: 처음이에요 (cheoeum-ieyo = it's my first time).

english: It's my first time in Korea.

grammar: 해요체 doubles as 'let's': 같이 마셔요 (gachi masyeoyo = let's drink together).

english: Do you have a business card?
I've heard a lot about you.
grammar: 말씀 많이 들었어요 (malsseum mani deureosseoyo) = 'I've heard a lot about you' — a warm meeting phrase.

english: I'll introduce my family this weekend.
